(2) My own stdlib script (scratchpad sensing-imutemp/recompute.py, no import of the subject), built from IEEE Std 952 angle variance N^2 T + K^2 T^3/3, the equicorrelated-mean variance identity and the ramp integral c*r*T^2/2, brute-forces n: table A rows 0/0.01/0.03/0.1/0.3/1.0 degC/min give k=3 n = 9/10/10/15/never/never and k=10 n = 100/106/195/never, floors 0.00167/0.005/0.01667/0.05/0.16667 deg and single-unit RMS 0.07071...0.37933, all equal to results.txt; tables C (f=0.5 -> 4, f=0.2 -> 1) and D (f=1, 0.5 never; 0.1 -> 15; 0.02 -> 10) equal. The arithmetic is right; the scope condition behind the headline is a claims defect, not a numerical one.

evidence.claims: Checked: '9 tests' (pass), floor formula mu*r*T^2/2 (pass, model.py:44), '3x unit cannot be matched above 0.2 degC/min' (pass, asymptote 0.212), '10x above 0.04' (pass, 0.0435), 'near k^2 only at about 2% residual' (pass, table D), 'Monte Carlo within 1% RMS' (pass, max 0.66%), 'Produced with AI assistance' disclosed, assumptions disclosed. Fail: the opening answer 'no, once the ramp is fast enough' is stated generally, but it only holds when mu^2(k^2-1) > s^2; with the README's own mu=0.002, s=0.004 a 2x better unit is ALWAYS matchable (recompute.py: k=2 needs 15/16/16 units at 1/10/100 degC/min, never infeasible). The condition is not disclosed. Also 'Builds on' cites only two in-repo projects; no external prior work is cited, so novelty is implied by omission.
evidence.fitness: Nearest prior work: Bayard & Ploen, 'High accuracy inertial sensors from inexpensive components' (JPL, US Patent 6,882,964, 2005), and the virtual-gyro line (Chang, Xue et al., Kalman fusion of correlated MEMS gyro arrays); Skog, Nilsson, Handel & Nehorai, 'Inertial sensor arrays, maximum likelihood, and Cramer-Rao bound', IEEE Trans. Signal Process. 2016, and Nilsson & Skog's 2016 array literature review, which already treat correlated errors as the limit of array averaging. The result here is the standard equicorrelated-mean identity Var = sigma^2(1-rho)/n + rho sigma^2 with rho supplied by a common tempco: sound, but not new, and not checked on any real gyro data. Parameters mu and s are invented although bias-over-temperature figures are published in consumer gyro datasheets (research/CLAUDE.md, 'Run the numbers; don't stylise them'). A researcher gets a correct 97-line model and nothing beyond a textbook formula; not in PROGRAMMES.md (legacy_projects.txt:837), far from the PhD-level programme bar.
evidence.domain: Against IEEE Std 952 noise terms and standard MEMS thermal-calibration practice. Departures a senior INS engineer hits first: (a) a fixed, grade-level shared tempco mu is exactly what factory or lot-level thermal calibration removes using the on-die temperature sensor every MEMS IMU has, so the uncompensated case is the least realistic one, yet it carries the headline; (b) compensation scales mu and s by the same f, whereas the common mean is far easier to fit than per-unit spread; (c) mu is a fixed offset, not a lot-to-lot random variable, so 'RMS' mixes a deterministic bias with noise; (d) a linear ramp only, no hysteresis or inter-unit gradients (disclosed). The noise terms and ramp integral themselves are textbook-correct.

defects.what: Headline 'no, once the ramp is fast enough' is stated generally but holds only when mu^2(k^2-1) > s^2; with the README's own mu=0.002, s=0.004 a 2x better unit is matchable at every ramp (15-16 units). Condition undisclosed. Fix: after the first bold sentence add 'This needs the shared tempco to dominate: mu^2(k^2-1) > s^2. With the illustrative mu = 0.002 and s = 0.004 that holds for k >= 3 but not k = 2, where 16 units always suffice.'

No external prior work cited; the floor is the textbook equicorrelated-mean variance, and gyro-array correlated-error limits are treated in Bayard & Ploen (2005) and Skog et al. (IEEE TSP 2016). Fix: add a 'Prior work' line naming them and stating the contribution is a tempco-mechanism parametrisation of rho, not a new result.

Shared tempco mu and spread s, which set every headline threshold, are invented ('both assumptions') although bias-over-temperature specs are published in consumer MEMS gyro datasheets; no sweep over mu/s shows whether the conclusion survives (it does not for s > mu*sqrt(k^2-1)).

Headline case leaves the grade-level shared tempco uncompensated, and compensation scales mu and s by the same f; in practice the common mean is removed first by lot/factory thermal calibration using the on-die temperature sensor, so the modelled floor mostly describes an uncalibrated system.

No test pins the better grade's tempco scaling or any headline number: mutant mu/k -> mu/sqrt(k) survives, as does ceil -> round in units_needed. Fix: add a test asserting units_needed(CHEAP, better_grade(CHEAP,3), 100, 0.1/60) == 15 and max_ramp_for_tie(..., 90, 100)*60 ~= 0.192.

verdict: Arithmetic is right and fully reproducible: run.py and figure.py regenerate results.txt and floor.svg byte-for-byte, and my own brute-force script, closed-form asymptote (0.2121 and 0.0435 degC/min for k = 3 and 10) and an independent rate-domain Monte Carlo all agree with the published tables. It falls short as research: the 'floor' is the textbook equicorrelated-mean variance with rho supplied by a shared tempco, no gyro-array literature is cited, mu and s are invented, the uncompensated shared-tempco case a practitioner would calibrate away carries the headline, and the headline's 'no' silently needs mu^2(k^2-1) > s^2 (false for k = 2 with its own parameters). Two of five seeded mutants survive. Does not meet the bar; finished for what it claims.
